title: Simulacro 10 — Security architecture: Zero Trust, secrets, IAM, network design
focus: Zero Trust, least privilege, defense-in-depth, secrets management (Vault/SSM/Secrets Manager), IAM policies traps, network segmentation, VPC design, TLS everywhere, JWT vs sessions.

questions.scenario: CEO leyó sobre Zero Trust y quiere implementarlo. Un colega dice: 'ya usamos VPN, es lo mismo'. Otro: 'Zero Trust = solo mTLS'.
questions.question: ¿Cuál es la DEFINICIÓN correcta de Zero Trust?

options.text: Zero Trust = eliminar VPN.
options.why: Simplistic. Zero Trust puede reemplazar VPN en algunos casos (BeyondCorp) pero no es 'eliminar VPN'. Es un modelo arquitectural más amplio.

options.text: Zero Trust es un modelo donde NUNCA se asume trust basado en location (network perimeter). Cada request es autenticado, autorizado, y encriptado independientemente. Principios: (1) verify explicitly (identidad + contexto de cada request); (2) least privilege access (permisos mínimos, JIT/JEA); (3) assume breach (segmentation, monitoring, encryption). NIST SP 800-207 formaliza. Implementación combina: mTLS everywhere, strong identity (SSO + MFA), context-aware policies, micro-segmentation, continuous verification.
options.why: Correcto. NIST SP 800-207 'Zero Trust Architecture' (2020) es el standard framework. Traditional network security: 'perimeter' (VPN, firewall) — inside trusted, outside untrusted. Once inside, movement lateral fácil. Zero Trust: (a) No implicit trust based on network location. (b) Every request authenticated + authorized. (c) Access based on identity + context + resource, not IP. (d) Continuous verification (not one-time login). (e) Micro-segmentation limits lateral movement. Implementación NO es una sola tecnología — es approach architectural. Ver Google BeyondCorp (pionero), Microsoft Zero Trust framework, CISA guidance.

options.text: Zero Trust = usar VPN + firewall más estrictos.
options.why: Este es 'perimeter security' (traditional). Zero Trust intenta reemplazar/complementar el modelo perimeter con enfoque based on identity + context, NO on network location. Fundamentally different.

options.text: Zero Trust = todo requiere MFA.
options.why: MFA es UNA pieza (strong authentication). Zero Trust es holístico: authentication + authorization + micro-segmentation + encryption + continuous verification + monitoring.

questions.explanation: Zero Trust (Forrester's John Kindervag 2010, formalized NIST SP 800-207 2020, popularized by Google BeyondCorp 2011+): fundamental shift from perimeter-based security. Principles: (1) Never trust, always verify — no implicit trust from network location. Corporate network is not automatically 'trusted'. (2) Least privilege — access to specific resources only, JIT (just-in-time) access. (3) Assume breach — attacker will get in; limit blast radius. (4) Continuous verification — reauthenticate, reauthorize based on context changes. Implementation components: (a) Strong identity — SSO (SAML, OIDC), MFA, hardware keys (FIDO2/WebAuthn). (b) Device trust — device compliance, EDR posture. (c) Least privilege access — IAM with fine-grained permissions, PAM (privileged access management). (d) Micro-segmentation — network isolation between services (mTLS, service mesh policies). (e) Encryption everywhere — TLS/mTLS in transit, encryption at rest. (f) Continuous monitoring — SIEM, UEBA, anomaly detection. (g) Context-aware policies — access considers user, device, location, time, resource sensitivity. Google BeyondCorp: employees access apps directly (no VPN); access decisions per-request based on user + device state. Not migration you do once — journey years.
questions.realWorld: Google BeyondCorp is canonical case study (papers, 2011-2018). Cloudflare Zero Trust (Access, Gateway). Microsoft Zero Trust framework. NIST SP 800-207. US federal government Executive Order 14028 (2021) mandating Zero Trust. Post-SolarWinds/Colonial Pipeline attacks accelerated adoption. Estimated 60%+ enterprises pursuing Zero Trust 2024.

references.title: Google — 'BeyondCorp: A New Approach to Enterprise Security' papers

questions.scenario: Team AWS otorga policy `s3:*` on `*` a Lambda function 'para que funcione'. Security team objeta. Team dice: 'es solo interno, no importa'.
questions.question: ¿Cuáles son los problemas concretos y cómo hacerlo bien?

options.text: 'Interno' no es defensa: (1) si Lambda tiene vulnerability (log4shell, dependency compromise), attacker gana s3:* — leak ALL buckets in account (incluyendo backups sensibles, audit logs), delete data, ransom. (2) Insider threat — dev con acceso a modify Lambda code puede exfiltrate. (3) Compliance (SOC2, ISO 27001, PCI) require least privilege. Hacer bien: policy con Action: [s3:GetObject], Resource: arn:aws:s3:::specific-bucket/specific-prefix/*. Use AWS Access Analyzer to identify unused permissions.
options.why: Correcto. Least privilege es defensa contra: (1) Compromise (código malicioso, vulnerabilities, credential leak). (2) Misconfiguration (bugs affecting wrong resources). (3) Insider threat. (4) Compliance requirements. AWS Access Analyzer genera policies based on actual usage (last 90 days) — starting point for restriction. IAM policies deben especificar: Actions específicas (not *), Resources específicos (not *), Conditions cuando aplicable (source IP, MFA required, time).

options.text: Interno = no risk, wildcards OK.
options.why: Falso. Interno reduce (some) risk pero no elimina. Vulnerabilities en dependencies (npm, pip) get exploited. Insider threat exists. Regulaciones requieren least privilege regardless. 'Interno' es rationalization.

options.text: Otorgar admin y monitor cambios.
options.why: Monitoring es detective (find breach after happens); least privilege es preventive (limit blast radius). Both needed, ni uno sustituye el otro. Admin + monitoring = 'find out we were breached badly'.

options.text: Otorgar temporary access con expiración.
options.why: JIT access es una opción para humans (Vault, AWS SSO) pero Lambdas necesitan permissions ejecutar. Debe ser scoped mínimo permanentemente, not 'temporary admin'.

questions.explanation: IAM least privilege in cloud: (1) AWS: IAM policies con specific Actions + Resources + Conditions. Avoid wildcards. Use Access Analyzer to identify used permissions. (2) GCP: predefined roles vs custom. Prefer predefined narrow (roles/pubsub.subscriber not roles/pubsub.admin). (3) Azure: RBAC with narrow roles. Custom roles for edge cases. Common traps: (a) `s3:*`, `iam:*`, `*:*` — full access to entire service. (b) Resource `*` — all resources of that type. (c) `iam:PassRole` on `*` — can assign any role. Privilege escalation vector. (d) Trust policy overly permissive — allow any account/user assume. (e) NotAction — dangerous, often reversed logic. Tools: (a) AWS IAM Access Analyzer — generate policies from CloudTrail history. (b) Cloudsplaining — analyze IAM policies for risks. (c) Prowler, ScoutSuite — cloud security auditing. (d) Cloud Custodian — policy-as-code enforcement. Zero Trust extension: SCP (Service Control Policies) en AWS Organizations set guardrails no accounts can bypass. Permission boundaries limit maximum permissions. Defense in depth.
questions.realWorld: Capital One breach (2019): SSRF vulnerability + overly permissive IAM = 100M+ records leaked. Attacker used compromised role to enum + exfil S3. IAM restrictions would've limited blast. Uber breach (2016): AWS keys in GitHub repo + broad permissions = 57M records. AWS Access Analyzer is direct response to widespread over-permissioning. Common finding: 80%+ of IAM permissions unused (research by CyberArk, others).

questions.scenario: App accede a DB con password. Actualmente hardcoded en config file committed to git. Team migra a Kubernetes y busca solución.
questions.question: ¿Cuáles son opciones profesionales y trade-offs?

options.text: Kubernetes Secrets (native) — base64-encoded (NO encrypted by default en etcd) — better than plaintext pero limited. External Secrets Operator sync desde AWS Secrets Manager / HashiCorp Vault / GCP Secret Manager — real encryption + rotation + audit. Sealed Secrets (Bitnami) — encrypted en git, decrypted en cluster. Vault Agent injection — sidecar/init inject secrets sin nunca tocar disco. Elegir: PaaS (AWS SM), Kubernetes-native (Sealed Secrets), enterprise multi-cloud (Vault).
options.why: Correcto. Options: (1) K8s Secrets — baseline. base64 (NOT encryption). Enable etcd encryption at rest. Kubelet reads y expone as env vars or volumes. Better than plaintext, insufficient alone. (2) External Secrets Operator (ESO) — sync from managed KMS/vaults into K8s Secrets. Central source of truth outside cluster. Rotation possible. (3) Sealed Secrets (Bitnami) — GitOps-friendly: encrypt secrets con cluster's public key, commit ciphertext to git, controller decrypts on apply. (4) Vault Agent — sidecar/init container injects secrets. Auto-renewal, no disk persistence. (5) CSI driver (Secrets Store CSI Driver) — mount secrets as volume from external. Elegir per context.

options.text: Kubernetes Secrets están encriptados by default.
options.why: Falso. Kubernetes Secrets son base64-encoded en etcd. Base64 no es encryption (es solo encoding). Etcd encryption at rest debe enabled explicitly (KMS provider config).

options.text: Env vars en deployment YAML committed en git.
options.why: Empeora la situación. Git history preserva plaintext secret forever, incluso si deleted (git filter-branch parcialmente resuelve). Diff públicos si repo público. Anti-patrón universal.

options.text: Env vars pasadas via kubectl create secret --from-literal.
options.why: Créate secrets manually via kubectl no es GitOps (secret state doesn't match git). Además leaves secret in shell history, log de kubectl audit. Better: managed secrets sync automatically.

questions.explanation: Secrets management arquitecturalmente crítico. Options ecosystem: (1) Kubernetes Secrets (native): base64 encoded (not encrypted); etcd encryption at rest opcional (recommend enable con KMS provider); RBAC restricts access; pods mount as env or volume. Baseline. (2) External Secrets Operator: sync from AWS Secrets Manager / GCP Secret Manager / Azure Key Vault / HashiCorp Vault / others into K8s Secrets. Centralized outside cluster. Rotation via external system. (3) Sealed Secrets (Bitnami): asymmetric encryption. Encrypt with cluster's public key (offline). Commit encrypted YAML to git. In-cluster controller decrypts to K8s Secret. GitOps-friendly. (4) Vault: HashiCorp Vault, industry standard for secrets. Features: dynamic secrets (generate per request, short TTL), transit encryption, PKI, database credentials rotation. Vault Agent sidecar/init injects secrets to pod file system (no k8s Secret intermediate). (5) CSI Secrets Store: mount secrets as volume from external providers. Considerations: (a) Rotation — how often secrets rotate, impact on app (need reload?). (b) Access audit — who accessed secret when. (c) Encryption in transit — HTTPS between pod and secret source. (d) Blast radius — service account per pod, minimal permissions. (e) Emergency access — break-glass procedures. Modern default: Vault or cloud-native secrets manager + operator.
questions.realWorld: HashiCorp Vault used by Fortune 500 extensively. AWS Secrets Manager tightly integrated with Lambda/ECS. Bitnami Sealed Secrets popular in GitOps workflows. Doppler, Infisical modern SaaS alternatives. Secret sprawl (secrets in multiple systems) is common enterprise problem — centralize.

questions.scenario: New app authentication. Team debate: JWT (stateless) vs server-side sessions (stateful) para user auth.
questions.question: ¿Cuáles son los trade-offs y cuándo cada uno?

options.text: JWT siempre — es moderno y stateless.
options.why: Simplificación. JWT tiene real problems: (1) revocation difficult (token valid until expiry, no server-side blacklist without additional infra); (2) size grande (bytes, in every request); (3) content puede leak if intercepted (encrypt-then-sign helps); (4) key management critical. Sessions won't scale trivially but for many apps are simpler.

options.text: Trade-offs: JWT — stateless (no server session store), scale-friendly, but revocation difícil (need blocklist infra), tokens grandes, expiration puede leak long time. Sessions — stateful (Redis/DB session store), revocation trivial (delete session), smaller cookie (session ID), well-understood security model. JWT bueno para: microservicios (pass identity across services), mobile APIs, short-lived contexts. Sessions bueno para: server-rendered web apps, cuando need instant revocation, long-lived sessions. Combinar: JWT with short TTL (5-15 min) + refresh token stored server-side (revocable). OAuth2 patterns.
options.why: Correcto y matizado. Ambos tienen use cases legítimos. JWT: self-contained (signature verifiable without server check), stateless (no lookup), pero revocation es problema (compromiso = valid until expiry). Sessions: server has state, revocation instant, session ID opaque. Modern pattern: JWT access token (short TTL, 5-15 min) + refresh token (long TTL, revocable stored server-side). OAuth 2.0 formalizes. OWASP recommendations para each. Elegir based on requirements.

options.text: Sessions siempre — más seguras.
options.why: También simplificación. Sessions al scale requiren coordinated session store (Redis cluster, DB), sticky sessions o distributed. Trade-offs exist both directions.

options.text: Cookies plain sin sessions.
options.why: Vulnerable a tampering (client puede modify). Sessions or signed cookies (Rails, Django default) needed. JWT itself es signed cookie in disguise.

questions.explanation: JWT vs sessions is nuanced auth architecture decision. JWT (JSON Web Token): self-contained token con claims (user ID, expiration, roles) signed with HMAC (HS256) or asymmetric (RS256). Verifiable without server state. Pros: (1) Stateless — scale trivially. (2) Cross-service — pass identity between microservicios. (3) Mobile-friendly — no cookie complexity. Cons: (1) Revocation hard — valid until expiry. Blocklist adds state (defeats stateless benefit). (2) Size — hundreds bytes vs session ID ~20-40 chars. Every request pays. (3) Content in payload — can be inspected (base64, not encrypted). Sensitive claims should be encrypted (JWE) or omitted. (4) Key rotation complex. (5) Vulnerabilities historically: none/alg confusion attacks (2015), key confusion. Sessions: server stores session data (Redis, DB), client has opaque session ID cookie. Pros: (1) Revocation trivial — delete server-side. (2) Small cookie. (3) Well-understood security. Cons: (1) Server state — need session store. (2) Session store availability critical. Modern combo (OAuth 2.0): (a) Short-lived access token (JWT, 5-15 min) — stateless, expires soon. (b) Refresh token (long-lived, revocable, stored server) — get new access token. (c) Best of both. When access token compromised, damage limited (short TTL). Revocation via refresh token deletion.
questions.realWorld: Auth0, Okta, AWS Cognito, Firebase Auth follow OAuth 2.0 pattern. Twitter API uses OAuth. GitHub uses hybrid. Rails/Django default to sessions, add JWT for API. React apps often JWT + refresh token pattern. Choose based on your architecture: microservicios need cross-service identity (JWT), monolith is fine with sessions. Security-critical apps favor sessions for revocation.

questions.scenario: Sistema tiene TLS en el edge (Cloudflare) pero internal service-to-service es HTTP plain 'porque está en VPC private'.
questions.question: ¿Por qué es necesario TLS/mTLS INTERNO también?

options.text: 'VPC private' no es garantía de safe. Zero Trust: assume breach. Threats internos: (1) compromised pod puede sniff otro traffic (network sniffing); (2) misconfigured routing exposes internal traffic; (3) shared cloud tenancy — otras cargas del mismo tenant potentially; (4) insider threat; (5) compliance (PCI, HIPAA) require encryption in transit. mTLS additionally provides mutual authentication: server AND client verify certificates → prevents server-side spoofing y provides identity for authorization. Service mesh (Istio, Linkerd) automatizan mTLS between services.
options.why: Correcto. 'Perimeter security' (protect boundary, trust internal) obsolete. Threats: (a) Lateral movement post-breach — attacker gains one pod, sniffs internal traffic. (b) Insider threat — malicious admin. (c) Misconfiguration — routing bug exposes internal. (d) Cloud infrastructure — shared hardware, hypervisor bugs (rare but possible). (e) Compliance requires encryption in transit. mTLS: both sides authenticate. Server proves identity (has cert signed by trusted CA). Client also proves identity. Enables service-to-service authentication + encryption in one mechanism. Service mesh (Istio, Linkerd) automate cert distribution + rotation.

options.text: VPC private es totalmente safe — no need TLS.
options.why: Perimeter mindset. VPC is admin domain con reduced attack surface pero not zero. Modern security assumes breach y layers defenses (defense-in-depth).

options.text: TLS interno solo si datos regulados (PCI, HIPAA).
options.why: Compliance is one driver pero not sole. Best practice regardless. Cost of mTLS with service mesh es low; benefits significant.

options.text: IPsec o WireGuard entre nodes — no mTLS.
options.why: Network-level encryption (IPsec) protects hop-to-hop pero not application-level identity. mTLS provides identity (X.509 certs) tied to service, enables fine-grained authz. Complementary, but mTLS more granular.

questions.explanation: TLS everywhere / mTLS internal: (1) TLS in transit — encrypts data on wire. Protects against sniffing, MITM. Public internet: mandatory (Let's Encrypt makes it free). Internal networks: increasingly best practice. (2) mTLS (mutual TLS) — both sides authenticate. Server proves identity (like public TLS), client also proves. Enables: (a) Service identity — 'this request comes from service X pod Y'. (b) Authorization based on identity — Envoy filters, service mesh policies. (c) Encryption without additional layer. Implementation: (a) Manual — issue certs from internal CA (private PKI), distribute, rotate. Complex operationally. (b) Service mesh — Istio, Linkerd, Consul Connect automate. Auto-inject sidecar (Envoy) that handles TLS. Cert issuance/rotation automatic. Policy declarative. (c) SPIFFE/SPIRE — cross-platform identity standard. Considerations: (a) Performance — TLS handshake overhead (mitigated by connection pooling). Modern hardware AES-NI negligible impact. (b) Cert management — expiring certs cause outages. Automate rotation (cert-manager, service mesh). (c) Legacy apps — may not support HTTPS. Use ambassador/sidecar to add TLS transparently. (d) Debugging — encrypted traffic harder to inspect. mTLS mandatory in NIST Zero Trust, common in modern architectures.
questions.realWorld: Google BeyondCorp: mTLS internal service-to-service via ALTS. Netflix uses mTLS extensively. Kubernetes admission webhooks require TLS. Cloud provider load balancers support end-to-end TLS. Istio, Linkerd defaults mTLS between meshed services. Companies migrating to Zero Trust: Cisco, Microsoft, big banks. Compliance (PCI DSS 4.0 explicit encryption in transit including internal).

references.title: SPIFFE — 'Secure Production Identity Framework for Everyone'

questions.scenario: Diseñas VPC para app nueva en AWS. Team pregunta: ¿public subnets solo, o VPC compleja con public/private/database subnets?
questions.question: ¿Cuál es el pattern recomendado y por qué?

options.text: Un subnet public + todo dentro. Simple.
options.why: Anti-pattern: exposes internal services (DBs, caches) directly to internet if security groups misconfigured. Defense-in-depth requires isolation. Also compliance requires internal-only for sensitive data.

options.text: 3-tier VPC: (1) Public subnets — internet-facing (ALB/NLB, NAT gateways). (2) Private subnets — app servers (no direct internet inbound; egress via NAT). (3) Database/data subnets — no internet access (VPC endpoints para AWS services, security groups restrict a app subnets). Multi-AZ replication de cada tier. Complementar: security groups (stateful firewall per instance), NACLs (subnet-level stateless), VPC flow logs, VPC endpoints (private access to S3/DynamoDB/etc sin internet).
options.why: Correcto. Standard 3-tier VPC pattern: (1) Public — internet-facing components solo (ALB, NAT). (2) Private — app tier. Can egress via NAT (updates, external APIs) but no inbound from internet. (3) Isolated data tier — DBs, caches. No egress ideally (VPC endpoints for AWS services). Security groups per instance (stateful, allow rules only). NACLs subnet-level (stateless, allow+deny, backstop). Multi-AZ (3 AZs typical) for HA. VPC endpoints (Gateway for S3/DDB, Interface for others) keep traffic private, no internet hops. VPC flow logs for audit/forensics.

options.text: Cada app en su propio VPC, no shared.
options.why: Sobre-fragmenta. Multi-VPC (transit gateway) apropiado para separación organizational (dev/staging/prod, or business units), not per app. Introduce cost + complexity. Single VPC bien segmentado por subnets es suficiente for most cases.

options.text: Serverless (Lambda) not need VPC.
options.why: Lambdas outside VPC hablan public internet (privado APIs need VPC config). Lambdas in VPC access private resources (RDS, ElastiCache). VPC design still matters — Lambdas típicamente en private subnets con VPC endpoints para AWS services.

questions.explanation: VPC design principles: (1) Segmentation by trust level — public (internet-facing), private (backend), isolated (data). Each tier communicates only necessary. (2) Multi-AZ — spread each tier across 3 AZs (typical) for HA. Subnet per AZ per tier = 9 subnets minimum (3 AZs × 3 tiers). (3) Security groups — instance-level firewall. Stateful. Reference other security groups (not IPs) for dynamic sizing. Explicit allow, deny by default. (4) NACLs — subnet-level, stateless, allow + deny. Broader net. Use as backup/enforcement. Explicit deny for known-bad. (5) NAT Gateway — private → public egress. Costly if bandwidth high; sometimes VPC endpoints eliminate need. (6) VPC endpoints — private connectivity to AWS services (S3, DDB, SQS, etc.). Traffic stays in AWS backbone, no internet cost. Gateway endpoints free; Interface endpoints hourly. (7) VPC peering — connect VPCs (own account or cross). Transit Gateway for hub-and-spoke multi-VPC. (8) Flow logs — record accepted/rejected connections. CloudWatch/S3 destination for analysis. (9) DNS — Route 53 private hosted zones for internal DNS. Considerations: (a) IPv4 CIDR planning — avoid overlaps (future peering). Use RFC1918 (10.x, 172.16.x, 192.168.x). (b) Cost — NAT Gateway ~$45/mo + data. Endpoints often cheaper. (c) Complexity — networking becomes complex quickly. Terraform/CDK for IaC.
questions.realWorld: Netflix uses complex VPC segmentation across accounts. Airbnb similar. AWS Landing Zone / Control Tower automate multi-account/VPC bootstrapping following best practices. Compliance requires (PCI DSS: segregation of cardholder data environment). VPC misconfigurations cause breaches (Capital One 2019: SSRF from misconfigured WAF + IAM).

questions.scenario: Team implementa WAF (Cloudflare) delante de app. Dev dice: 'con WAF, no necesitamos validation en el backend porque WAF filtra ataques'.
questions.question: ¿Por qué es incorrecto y qué principio aplica?

options.text: Es correcto: WAF es primera línea, backend puede confiar.
options.why: Anti-security. Single point of protection (WAF) = single point of failure. WAF bypasses exist (HTTP smuggling, WAF misconfiguration, novel attacks). Backend trust of WAF-filtered input is single-layer defense — fragile.

options.text: Defense in Depth (Bell-LaPadula, NIST): security debe ser en MÚLTIPLES layers. Si WAF fails/bypassed, backend validation catches. Layers típicos: (1) WAF/edge — DDoS, common exploits. (2) API Gateway — auth, rate limit, schema validation. (3) App validation — business logic, sanitization. (4) DB parameterized queries — prevent SQLi even if input validated poorly. (5) Encryption at rest, in transit. (6) Least privilege IAM. Cada layer independently effective. Attacker debe bypass todas.
options.why: Correcto. Defense in Depth (concept from military) es fundamental principle. Reason: (a) Single controls fail (bugs, bypasses, misconfig). (b) Attackers escalate — one weakness alone shouldn't be catastrophic. (c) Layered controls independently effective. Examples: (1) WAF filters attacks + backend validates input + parameterized queries + least privilege DB user. Attacker needs bypass ALL to succeed. (2) MFA + strong passwords + rate limiting + anomaly detection. (3) Network segmentation + host firewall + encryption + application authorization. Modern security frameworks (NIST CSF, ISO 27001) enforce layered controls.

options.text: Confiar en cada layer separately.
options.why: Wrong direction. Cada layer INDIVIDUALLY should validate. No trust cross-layer — assume previous layer failed.

options.text: One perfect layer suficiente si diseñado bien.
options.why: No layer es perfect. Novel attacks, misconfigurations, insider threats exist. Layered defense is fundamental.

questions.explanation: Defense in Depth: multiple independent security controls at different layers. Even if one fails, others prevent full compromise. Concept from military (multiple lines of defense, not just perimeter). In IT security: (1) Network layer — firewalls, WAF, DDoS protection, segmentation, IPS/IDS. (2) Host layer — OS hardening, EDR, HIDS, file integrity monitoring. (3) Application layer — input validation, output encoding, authentication, authorization, session management, error handling. (4) Data layer — encryption at rest, encryption in transit, DLP, database security (parameterized queries, least privilege), backups. (5) Monitoring/detection — SIEM, log aggregation, anomaly detection, alerting. (6) Response — IR plan, forensics readiness. (7) Identity — MFA, SSO, PAM, privileged access review. Common failures: (a) 'WAF catches all attacks' — SQLi bypasses via encoding tricks. (b) 'Firewall prevents intrusion' — insider or compromised credential bypasses. (c) 'DB is internal so no encryption needed' — breach exposes plaintext. (d) 'Small system doesn't need monitoring' — silent compromise. Modern implementations: NIST Cybersecurity Framework, CIS Controls, MITRE ATT&CK for threat modeling. Layered defense assumed baseline.
questions.realWorld: Target 2013 breach: HVAC vendor credentials compromised → lateral movement → POS malware → 40M cards. Multiple layer failures: no network segmentation isolating vendor access, no anomaly detection, no encryption of card data in memory. Any one layer catching would've prevented. Colonial Pipeline 2021: VPN password leaked → no MFA → ransomware full compromise. MFA layer would've prevented. Defense in depth prevents such single-point failures.

questions.scenario: Code review reveals: `db.query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = "' + userInput + '"')`. Dev dice: 'user tiene que estar authenticated, no puede ser malicious'.
questions.question: ¿Cuál es la vulnerabilidad y solución?

options.text: SQL Injection (OWASP A03:2021). Authenticated users también pueden be malicious (compromised account, insider, or app logic bugs elevating attack). Solución: parameterized queries (prepared statements). `db.query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = ?', [userInput])`. DB engine parses query separately from data — data cannot alter query structure. NUNCA concatenate user input into SQL string.
options.why: Correcto. SQL Injection sigue siendo TOP 10 después de 20+ años. Authenticated no is defense — compromised account, XSS + CSRF chain, insider threat. Parameterized queries: query template and parameters sent separately to DB. DB ensures params treated as data. Works in every language: PDO (PHP), psycopg2 (Python), sqlx (Go), Sequelize (Node), Hibernate (Java). ORM query builders also safe when used correctly (don't use raw() with concatenation).

options.text: Escape special characters como single quotes.
options.why: Manual escaping is error-prone: (1) Which characters to escape varies by DB (MySQL vs Postgres). (2) Charset issues (Unicode tricks). (3) Nested contexts (JSON in SQL string, etc.). Parameterized queries are DEFINITIVE solution — don't manual escape.

options.text: WAF filtrará SQL injection.
options.why: WAF may catch obvious attacks (`OR 1=1`) but bypass technique numerous: encoding, splits, timing-based blind SQL. WAF is defense-in-depth layer, not sole defense. Parameterized queries in code is definitive.

options.text: Aumentar user privileges to limit query results.
options.why: Inverso — MENOS privileges (least privilege) reduce impact but injection still occurs. Doesn't prevent, mitigates. Both parameterized queries + least privilege DB user (application user cannot DROP TABLE).

questions.explanation: OWASP Top 10 (2021): (1) A01 Broken Access Control — authz bugs (IDOR, missing checks). (2) A02 Cryptographic Failures — weak encryption, plaintext storage. (3) A03 Injection — SQL, NoSQL, LDAP, OS command injection. (4) A04 Insecure Design — architectural flaws. (5) A05 Security Misconfiguration — default creds, verbose errors, unpatched. (6) A06 Vulnerable Components — outdated libraries with known CVEs. (7) A07 Identification/Authentication Failures — weak auth, session mgmt. (8) A08 Software/Data Integrity Failures — CI/CD attacks, unsigned updates. (9) A09 Security Logging/Monitoring — missing audit trails. (10) A10 Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF). SQL injection specifically (A03): (a) Root cause: mixing code + data in same string. (b) Solution: parameterized queries separate them. (c) ORM defaults safe; raw queries dangerous. (d) Also: least privilege DB user (can't drop tables, can't access other schemas), monitoring for unusual queries. (e) Second-order injection: attacker stores payload, later query executes it. Solutions: (a) Parameterized queries EVERYWHERE. (b) Input validation (allowlist approach). (c) Output encoding (context-aware — HTML, JS, SQL). (d) Least privilege DB user. (e) WAF as defense-in-depth. (f) Regular code review + SAST tools (Semgrep, Snyk).
questions.realWorld: Equifax 2017: Apache Struts vuln → RCE → SQL access → 147M records. Yahoo 2013-14: injection contributed to 3B accounts. LinkedIn 2012: SQL injection → 6.5M passwords (unsalted MD5). British Airways 2018: injection via third-party JS. Constant reminder: injection is #1-#3 in every OWASP Top 10 since 2003. Modern static analysis (Semgrep, Snyk, GitHub CodeQL) catch many at dev time.

questions.scenario: AWS credentials para app hardcoded in env var since 2 años. Team dice: 'funcionan, no cambiar por si break'.
questions.question: ¿Por qué es problemático y qué approach moderno resuelve?

options.text: Credentials estáticas de larga vida son riesgo: (1) leak (git commit accidental, log leak, dev laptop stolen) exposes indefinitely; (2) revocation lag — al detectar breach, valid until rotated; (3) compliance (SOC2, PCI) require rotation. Modern: (1) IAM Roles for services (IRSA en EKS, Pod Identity, IAM instance profile) — auto-rotate credentials, no static keys. (2) OIDC federation (GitHub Actions OIDC to AWS) — short-lived tokens per workflow, no long-lived secret. (3) Vault dynamic secrets — generate per-request, short TTL, auto-revoke. (4) AWS Secrets Manager con rotation function. Move away from static keys.
options.why: Correcto. Static credentials + long-lived = massive risk. Modern architectures eliminate long-lived credentials wherever possible: (1) Service identity — AWS IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA) en EKS: pod assumes IAM role via OIDC, credentials auto-rotated by AWS SDK. Pod Identity (2023 GKE, EKS) similar. (2) Workload identity federation — GitHub Actions OIDC → AWS role: short-lived credential per workflow run. Eliminates PAT/access keys in CI/CD. (3) Vault dynamic secrets — DB credentials generated per request (5-min TTL), revoked automatically. Attacker window minimal. (4) AWS/GCP native rotation — Secrets Manager con Lambda rotation function auto-rotates DB creds, apps read from SM.

options.text: Static creds funcionan bien; rotation es unnecessary.
options.why: False security. Compromise inevitable eventually — question is how quickly detected + revoked. Static creds pueden persist years silently in stolen laptops, logs, git history. Rotation limits exposure window.

options.text: Rotar manually cada mes — sufficient.
options.why: Manual rotation error-prone, forgotten, breaks apps que hardcode. Automatic short-lived (hours or per-request) is superior. Modern cloud reduces or eliminates manual rotation entirely.

options.text: Cifrar el credential en env var.
options.why: 'Encrypted' env var still needs decryption key somewhere → chicken/egg. And once app decrypts, credential in memory. Static credential problem persists. Better: eliminate need for static credential (service identity, dynamic secrets).

questions.explanation: Credential management evolution: (1) Static long-lived credentials (bad) — API keys, passwords committed or in env vars. Rotate periodically manually. High risk of leak. (2) Managed rotation (better) — cloud secrets manager rotates automatically. App reads current from SM. Short window between rotation and next. (3) Service identity (best for services) — cloud IAM identity (IAM Role, Service Account) tied to workload. Auto-rotate short-lived credentials. No static credential. AWS IRSA, GCP Workload Identity, Azure Managed Identity. Kubernetes ServiceAccount + OIDC. (4) Workload federation — CI/CD workloads (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI) use OIDC to assume cloud role for that run. No long-lived credential in CI. (5) Dynamic secrets — Vault generates credentials per request. Short TTL (mins). App requests each time. Ideal for DB credentials. Common patterns: (a) AWS IRSA + secrets from Secrets Manager (rotated automatically). (b) GitHub Actions OIDC → AWS role → deploy. (c) Vault dynamic DB creds for app. (d) Human access via SSO + PAM (JIT elevation). Modern security posture: minimize static credentials, embrace service identity + short-lived tokens.
questions.realWorld: AWS re:Invent talks feature IRSA / Pod Identity extensively. GitHub launched OIDC to AWS 2021, adoption grew rapidly. HashiCorp Vault dynamic secrets used at Adobe, HashiCorp itself, many. Uber post-2016 breach adopted extensive dynamic secrets. GitHub Actions default OIDC to reduce PAT usage in CI.

references.title: GitHub Docs — 'Configuring OpenID Connect in AWS'

questions.topic: Encryption at rest — más allá de 'sí, tengo'
questions.scenario: Team dice 'AWS RDS es encrypted at rest, todo bien'. Auditor pregunta: ¿quién controla las keys? ¿cómo se rotan? ¿qué pasa si AWS es comprometido?
questions.question: ¿Cuáles son los NIVELES de encryption at rest en cloud?

options.text: Cloud provider managed keys (SSE-S3, RDS default): AWS controls keys totalmente. Simple, cero mantenimiento. Trust cloud provider. Bueno para non-sensitive. Customer Master Keys (CMK) en KMS: user manages key policy, rotation, audit. AWS aún has custody de material key (managed by KMS). Better control + audit. Customer-provided keys (SSE-C, external KMS, HYOK/BYOK): user provides key material. AWS cannot decrypt without user-provided key. Highest control, most operational overhead. Combining: envelope encryption — data encrypted con Data Encryption Key (DEK), DEK encrypted con KEK stored en KMS.
options.why: Correcto. Levels: (1) Provider-managed keys — provider controls entirely. Convenience, less control. Trust provider security. (2) Customer Managed Keys (CMK) in KMS — user controls policy, rotation schedule, access audit. Provider still hosts key material (safer than customer-hosted). Best balance for most. (3) BYOK (Bring Your Own Key) / HYOK (Hold Your Own Key) — user provides key material, provider uses. Provider cannot decrypt without user cooperation. High control, complex ops. Envelope encryption pattern: data encrypted con DEK (fast symmetric), DEK encrypted con KEK (in KMS, HSM-backed). Rotate KEK doesn't require re-encrypt all data. Common approach: KMS + envelope encryption.

options.text: 'Encrypted at rest' es equivalente todos los levels.
options.why: Fundamentally different in threat model. Provider-managed: protects against theft of physical disk. Customer keys: protects also against rogue cloud admin, compliance requirements. Consider threat model.

options.text: Solo BYOK provides real security.
options.why: Overkill for most cases. CMK in KMS is sufficient para most use cases + audit + rotation. BYOK adds significant operational burden (secure key generation, rotation, transport). Reserve for highest-sensitivity.

options.text: Application-level encryption elimina need for at-rest.
options.why: Complementary, not alternative. App-level encrypts specific fields (PII, credit cards) even from DBA. At-rest protects entire storage from physical/hypervisor attacks. Both valuable. Defense in depth.

questions.explanation: Encryption at rest layers: (1) Provider-managed (default) — cloud provider handles keys transparently. AES-256 typical. Protects against physical disk theft, disposal. Zero user config. Trust provider security. AWS S3 SSE-S3, RDS default. (2) Customer Managed Keys (CMK) — user creates KMS key, controls policy (who can use), rotation schedule, audit logs (CloudTrail records usage). Provider still hosts key in HSM. AWS KMS, GCP Cloud KMS, Azure Key Vault. Rotation: AWS auto-rotates yearly optionally; users control manual rotation. (3) BYOK/HYOK — user provides key material to cloud. Provider uses but cannot alone decrypt without user key. Higher control. Operational: key generation ceremony, secure transport, rotation. Overkill unless compliance mandates. Envelope encryption: (a) DEK — Data Encryption Key, symmetric (AES), fast for data. (b) KEK — Key Encryption Key, master key in KMS. Encrypts DEKs. (c) Rotate KEK without re-encrypting data — rewrap DEKs. Application-level encryption: encrypt specific fields (PII, cards) at app layer before DB. Extra protection: DBA cannot see plaintext. Complements at-rest. Compliance: PCI DSS requires encryption of cardholder data. HIPAA requires PHI encryption. GDPR encourages. GDPR pseudonymization.
questions.realWorld: AWS KMS (2014) revolucionó cloud encryption. GCP Cloud KMS, Azure Key Vault similar. HashiCorp Vault for multi-cloud + on-prem. Companies with compliance (PCI, HIPAA, financial) use CMK universally. Envelope encryption standard AWS pattern. BYOK niche but growing for regulated industries.

questions.scenario: New feature: payment processing. PM pregunta cómo evaluate risks. Team dice: 'seguimos best practices, no threat model needed'.
questions.question: ¿Qué es threat modeling y por qué useful?

options.text: Threat modeling: proceso systematic para identificar threats, vulnerabilities, mitigations. Frameworks: STRIDE (Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege), PASTA, LINDDUN (privacy). Steps: (1) diagram architecture (data flow diagrams); (2) identify assets + trust boundaries; (3) enumerate threats per component/data flow; (4) rate risks; (5) design mitigations. 'Best practices' es baseline, threat modeling identifica specific risks del sistema.
options.why: Correcto. Best practices are general (encrypt, MFA, validate input); threat modeling is specific to YOUR system. Reveals: (1) Trust boundaries misplaced. (2) Missing controls. (3) Attack paths overlooked. (4) Data flows exposed. STRIDE (Microsoft) es popular framework — cover main threat categories. Threat modeling en design phase catches issues before code (10-100x cheaper than fixing in production). Shift-left security.

options.text: 'Best practices' cover todo.
options.why: Falso. Best practices are baseline. Your system has specific attack surface, data flows, trust boundaries. Threat modeling identifies specific risks. Best practices catch common — modeling catches architectural-specific.

options.text: Threat modeling es for military/gov apps solo.
options.why: Falso. Any system con security requirements benefits. Payment processing especially — high value target, regulatory scrutiny. Microsoft SDL requires threat modeling for all products.

options.text: Do threat modeling after launch.
options.why: Backwards. Modeling in design phase is cheapest + most effective. Retrofitting security post-launch expensive + incomplete. Shift-left security.

questions.explanation: Threat modeling: (1) STRIDE (Microsoft, Kohnfelder-Garg 1999) — Spoofing (identity), Tampering (integrity), Repudiation (audit), Information disclosure (confidentiality), Denial of service (availability), Elevation of privilege. Enumerate each threat per component. (2) PASTA (Process for Attack Simulation and Threat Analysis) — 7-stage risk-centric. Deeper for enterprise. (3) LINDDUN — privacy-focused (GDPR era). (4) Attack trees — hierarchical decomposition of attack goals. (5) OCTAVE — organizational risk perspective. Process: (a) Define scope — feature, application, system. (b) Model — data flow diagram (DFD) showing components, data flows, trust boundaries. (c) Identify threats — apply STRIDE to each component/flow. Brainstorm what could go wrong. (d) Prioritize — DREAD (Damage, Reproducibility, Exploitability, Affected users, Discoverability) or similar. (e) Mitigate — controls to reduce risk. Design changes, monitoring, response. (f) Validate — test mitigations effective. Tools: Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool, OWASP Threat Dragon, IriusRisk. Best practice: threat model at design, revisit at major changes. Involve security team + architects + devs. Continuous, not one-time.
questions.realWorld: Microsoft SDL requires threat modeling for all products. Google Security Design Reviews. AWS Security review for major features. Financial services (PCI) require. Fintech, cloud providers, security-sensitive products mandate. STRIDE most widely used. IriusRisk automates.

references.title: Adam Shostack — 'Threat Modeling: Designing for Security'

questions.scenario: Nueva regulation post-SolarWinds attack requires attest to supply chain security. Team pregunta qué implica.
questions.question: ¿Qué componentes incluir en supply chain security?

options.text: Supply chain security cubre: (1) Dependencies scanning — Dependabot, Snyk, Trivy detect vulnerabilities en libraries. Update regularly. SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) manifiesto de todos components. (2) Build process — CI/CD hardening. Ephemeral runners, signed artifacts. SLSA framework niveles 1-4. (3) Artifact signing — Sigstore/Cosign firma container images, releases. Verify at deploy. (4) Provenance — attestations who/what built artifact, cual commit. (5) Dependency confusion attacks — private packages vs public typosquat. Use scopes, private registries. (6) Third-party components audit — vendor risk assessment. Log4shell (2021) y SolarWinds (2020) drove focus.
options.why: Correcto. Supply chain security holistic: (1) Dependencies — outdated libs con CVEs (Equifax = Struts). Automate scanning. Renovate/Dependabot for updates. Trivy/Snyk for container scans. (2) SBOM — CycloneDX or SPDX format listing all components + versions. Required by executive order for federal software. (3) Build supply chain — CI/CD is attack vector (compromised runner steals credentials, injects code). Ephemeral runners, isolated. SLSA framework (Google) has 4 levels. (4) Signing + attestations — Sigstore (CNCF), Cosign for signing container images. Verifies image is what was built by trusted party. (5) Provenance — SLSA Provenance attestation: 'this image was built from commit X, workflow Y, on date Z'. (6) Runtime — image scanning at admission (OPA, Kyverno).

options.text: Solo scan dependencies for vulns.
options.why: Incomplete. SolarWinds attack was compromise of build system (not dependency vuln). Log4shell was library vuln. Both matter. Supply chain includes build pipeline, artifacts, dependencies, third parties.

options.text: Encrypt everything.
options.why: Encryption is one control (protect artifact in transit). Doesn't address build pipeline compromise, dependency vulns, signing/attestation. Different threat model.

options.text: Use only trusted vendors.
options.why: Vendor trust is one element but insufficient. Even 'trusted' vendors get compromised (SolarWinds was trusted). Zero trust: verify, don't just trust. SBOM + signing + provenance verify continuously.

questions.explanation: Software supply chain security became critical concern post-SolarWinds (2020, Russia infiltrated build system, distributed malware to 18k customers) and Log4Shell (2021, log4j2 zero-day exploited widely). Executive Order 14028 (2021) mandated SBOM, secure development practices for federal software. Components: (1) Dependencies — SCA (Software Composition Analysis) tools (Snyk, Dependabot, Renovate, Trivy, Grype). Detect known vulns, license issues. Auto-update PRs. SBOM manifest. (2) Build pipeline — SLSA framework (Supply chain Levels for Software Artifacts, Google/OpenSSF). Levels 1-4 increasing rigor. Ephemeral runners (avoid persistent state compromise). Isolated builds. Signed provenance. (3) Artifact signing — Sigstore (Cosign, Rekor, Fulcio) provides keyless signing. Attestations of what was built. Notary (Docker) alternative. Verify signatures at deployment (admission controllers). (4) Provenance — attestations: 'This artifact hash X was built from commit Y, using workflow Z, on runner N at time T'. Verifiable chain of custody. SLSA Provenance format. (5) Third-party components audit — vendor risk assessments, penetration testing of dependencies. (6) Runtime protection — image scanning at admission, runtime detection (Falco, Tetragon). (7) Vulnerability disclosure programs — coordinated with vendors. OpenSSF (Open Source Security Foundation) drives standards. GitHub, GitLab, Azure integrate.
questions.realWorld: SolarWinds Orion (2020): build system compromised, malicious code in trusted software, 18k orgs affected including US federal. Log4Shell (Dec 2021): CVE-2021-44228 zero-day in log4j2, RCE via crafted log messages. Codecov (2021): CI/CD tool compromised, exfiltrated env vars from customer builds. These drove SLSA, Sigstore, executive orders. Google Distroless images, Chainguard Images provide hardened base.

questions.scenario: App permite users provide URL (e.g., avatar image URL). Backend fetches URL. Attacker provides `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/`. Backend returns EC2 metadata service response = IAM credentials.
questions.question: ¿Qué vulnerabilidad es y cómo prevenir?

options.text: SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery, OWASP A10:2021). Backend actúa como proxy para attacker, reaching internal resources normally inaccessible (metadata service, internal APIs, private networks). Prevención: (1) Validate URL — allowlist domains, block private IPs (127.0.0.1, 10.x, 169.254.x, ::1), block AWS metadata IP. (2) Fetch via proxy que enforces rules. (3) Disable HTTP redirects (attacker uses redirect to bypass). (4) IMDSv2 (AWS) requires token — mitigates este ataque específico. (5) Least privilege IAM role (Lambda/EC2 has minimum permissions).
options.why: Correcto. SSRF is one of most dangerous vulns cloud-era. Capital One 2019 breach: SSRF in WAF misconfiguration → attacker fetched IAM credentials via EC2 metadata → S3 access → 100M records. Prevention: (1) URL validation — allowlist better than blocklist. Reject private IPs (RFC1918, loopback, link-local 169.254.x). Special attention: 169.254.169.254 (AWS/GCP/Azure metadata). (2) Fetch layer — proxy with policies, or library configured to prevent (e.g., requests library con custom adapter validating). (3) Disable redirects OR follow with same validation. (4) IMDSv2 en AWS requires PUT to get session token before metadata — many SSRF only support GET, blocked. Enforce IMDSv2. (5) Least privilege IAM — even if attacker gets creds, minimal impact.

options.text: Solo backend sanitize input.
options.why: Sanitize what? Users legitimate provide URLs. Sanitization alone doesn't prevent SSRF — need URL validation + fetch controls. 'Sanitize' too vague.

options.text: SSRF no es un problema en cloud.
options.why: Cloud makes SSRF WORSE. Metadata services (IMDS) expose credentials. Internal services often accessible from within VPC. Capital One breach was direct SSRF in cloud.

options.text: WAF captures todos los SSRF attacks.
options.why: WAF pattern-matches specific attacks pero SSRF is application logic issue (backend fetches user-provided URL). WAF not primary control — code-level prevention essential.

questions.explanation: SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery): server fetches URL provided by user. Attacker abuses to access internal resources. Attack vectors: (1) Cloud metadata services — AWS IMDS (169.254.169.254), GCP metadata, Azure IMDS. Returns instance credentials, config. IMDSv1 required no auth — trivial to exploit. IMDSv2 (2019) requires token. (2) Internal services — /admin panels, internal APIs, databases exposed on private network. (3) Localhost services — Redis, Elasticsearch listening on 127.0.0.1 accessible only from same host. (4) Cloud provider APIs — from within cloud, some APIs accessible without auth. Prevention: (1) URL validation — allowlist domains, reject private IPs, reject metadata IPs specifically. (2) Fetch layer — proxy with policies. (3) Redirect handling — follow only to validated URLs, or don't follow. (4) DNS pinning — resolve DNS then use IP directly (prevents DNS rebinding attack). (5) Cloud metadata protection — IMDSv2 enforce. Instance profile with minimal permissions. (6) Network segmentation — services shouldn't have unfettered access to internal network. Egress firewall. Detection: monitor for unusual outbound requests, requests to metadata IPs, requests to private ranges.
questions.realWorld: Capital One 2019: SSRF in misconfigured WAF (Apache mod_security) + IAM role with excessive permissions = 100M+ credit card apps leaked. Exact attack: attacker sent request causing WAF to fetch metadata, revealed IAM credentials, used to S3 access. Post-breach: AWS pushed IMDSv2, education on SSRF prevention. Also blockchain platforms (Uniswap 2020) had SSRF-like issues. SSRF made OWASP Top 10 A10 in 2021.

references.title: OWASP — 'Server-Side Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet'
AWS — 'Add defense in depth against IMDS attacks'

questions.scenario: API pública sufre traffic sospechoso: mismo endpoint, 1000 rps de single IP. Team quiere protection.
questions.question: ¿Qué niveles de rate limiting/DDoS existen?

options.text: Layered defense: (1) CDN/edge (Cloudflare, CloudFront) — L3/L4 DDoS mitigation, L7 rate limiting. Absorbs volumétricos. (2) WAF — patrones + rate limits por rules. (3) API Gateway — per-user/per-endpoint rate limits (leaky bucket, token bucket). (4) App-level — business logic limits (X login attempts, N password resets/hour). Cada nivel targeteando distinto pattern. Volumetric al edge; application logic en app. Distinguir bot legítimo (search crawlers) from malicious.
options.why: Correcto. Rate limiting is layered: (1) CDN/edge DDoS — massive scale (Terabits) absorption. Cloudflare, AWS Shield, Akamai. L3/L4 volumetric attacks. (2) WAF — Layer 7 rules, rate limits per rule (Cloudflare WAF rules, AWS WAF rate-based rules). Block IPs exceeding threshold. (3) API Gateway — per-API-key/token limits. AWS API Gateway usage plans, Kong, Apigee. Token bucket typical. (4) Application — business logic (login attempts, password resets, expensive operations). Redis-based (INCR with TTL). Bot detection: rate + user-agent + fingerprint. Legitimate bots vs malicious behave differently.

options.text: Solo firewall block IP attacker.
options.why: Reactive, limited. Attacker uses botnet (10k+ IPs). Blocking individual IPs whack-a-mole. Rate limiting more scalable — allow legitimate traffic under threshold.

options.text: Aumentar capacity para absorber traffic.
options.why: Expensive escalation — attacker's cost is low, yours grows. Volumetric DDoS specifically designed to overwhelm capacity. Absorption at edge (CDN) is defense, not scaling app tier.

options.text: CAPTCHA en cada request.
options.why: Breaks legitimate UX. CAPTCHA specific to suspicious requests (challenge-response for detected bot activity), not blanket.

questions.explanation: Rate limiting + DDoS defense layered: (1) CDN/edge DDoS — Cloudflare, AWS Shield Advanced, Akamai. Absorbs volumetric (L3/L4 amplification, UDP floods) at edge. Terabits scale. Managed service. (2) WAF (Web Application Firewall) — pattern-based rules for L7 attacks (SQL injection, XSS). Rate-based rules for per-IP throttling. Cloudflare WAF, AWS WAF, ModSecurity. (3) API Gateway rate limiting — per-user/API-key limits. Token bucket (algo com constant refill + burst capacity) or leaky bucket. AWS API Gateway usage plans, Kong Community. (4) App-level rate limiting — business logic constraints. Redis with INCR + EXPIRE typical. Rack-attack (Rails), Flask-Limiter (Python), express-rate-limit (Node). Algorithms: (a) Fixed window — X requests per hour, resets. Simple, sudden reset boundary issue. (b) Sliding window — moving X-min window. Smoother. (c) Token bucket — tokens replenish at rate R, burst up to B. Allows bursts. (d) Leaky bucket — constant output rate. Considerations: (1) Distributed — rate limits must coordinate across app instances (Redis shared). (2) Bypass — auth users higher limit than anonymous. Admins bypass. (3) Communication — 429 Too Many Requests + Retry-After header. (4) Bot detection — Cloudflare Bot Management, fingerprinting. Distinguish good bots (Googlebot verified via reverse DNS). (5) SLI monitoring — rate limit hits indicate attack or misconfigured client.
questions.realWorld: GitHub, Stripe expose rate limits explicitly in headers (X-RateLimit-*). Cloudflare protects massive % of internet from DDoS. GitHub 2018 mitigated 1.35 Tbps memcached amplification attack. AWS Shield defended $2000+/mo customers from 2.3 Tbps attack 2020. API abuse (credential stuffing, scraping) uses rate limiting + fingerprinting.

questions.scenario: Team evalúa upgrade auth: mover de passwords + optional TOTP MFA a passwordless usando FIDO2/passkeys.
questions.question: ¿Cuáles son las ventajas y consideraciones?

options.text: Ventajas FIDO2/passkeys: (1) Phishing-resistant — cryptographic challenge-response bound to origin, cannot be phished to fake site. (2) No shared secrets — public key with server, private key on device. Breach doesn't leak credentials. (3) Better UX — no passwords to remember. Consideraciones: (1) Device recovery — losing device = losing account. Passkeys sync (Apple Keychain, Google Password Manager, 1Password) mitigate. (2) Migration — legacy users need path. (3) Attestation trade-off — knowing device type vs privacy. (4) Not universal support yet — older browsers/systems. Modern adoption: Google, Microsoft, Apple, GitHub, Cloudflare support passkeys 2023+.
options.why: Correcto. FIDO2 (WebAuthn + CTAP) formalizes phishing-resistant auth. Passkeys (2022 term) = FIDO2 credentials, syncing across devices. Advantages: (1) Phishing-resistant — origin binding (RP ID) means credential cannot be used on wrong domain. Fundamental security improvement over passwords/TOTP (both phishable). (2) No shared secret — server stores public key. Attacker with DB has useless data. (3) UX — Touch ID, Face ID, security keys. No typing passwords. Trade-offs: (1) Recovery — lost device = lost account without sync. Cloud-synced passkeys (Apple, Google) mitigate. (2) Device attestation vs privacy tension. (3) Fallback needed for old browsers/systems (still). (4) Multi-device account access.

options.text: Passwords siempre — más simple.
options.why: Passwords have decades of proven problems: phishing, reuse, weak choice, DB breaches, credential stuffing. FIDO2 addresses root causes. Simplicity < security in auth.

options.text: SMS OTP igual seguro.
options.why: SMS OTP vulnerable to SIM swapping (attacker takes over phone number), phishing (attacker relays OTP in real-time), telecom compromise. NIST deprecated SMS as MFA. FIDO2 much stronger.

options.text: TOTP (Google Authenticator) igual bien.
options.why: TOTP better than SMS but still phishable (attacker phishes OTP in real-time, uses within window). FIDO2 origin binding prevents phishing entirely. NIST recommends FIDO2/WebAuthn.

questions.explanation: FIDO2 (Fast IDentity Online 2, W3C + FIDO Alliance): (1) WebAuthn — browser API for authentication with public key crypto. (2) CTAP (Client to Authenticator Protocol) — communication with authenticators (security keys, biometric sensors, platform). Passkeys (2022+): FIDO2 credentials that sync across user devices via cloud (Apple Keychain, Google Password Manager, 1Password). Removes device-loss concern of traditional FIDO2. How it works: (1) Registration — client generates keypair, sends public to server + attestation. (2) Authentication — server sends challenge, client signs with private key (biometric/PIN prompt), sends signature. Server verifies. (3) Origin binding — credentials bound to RP ID (domain). Cannot use on wrong site. Fundamental phishing prevention. Comparison to passwords + MFA: (a) Passwords: server stores hash. Breach → offline cracking, credential stuffing. Phishable. (b) TOTP: shared secret. Phishable in real-time. Server breach exposes seeds. (c) SMS OTP: SIM swap attacks, telecom compromise. NIST deprecated. (d) FIDO2/passkeys: public key crypto, phishing-resistant, no shared secrets. Adoption 2024-2026: Apple, Google, Microsoft consumer products, GitHub, Cloudflare, banking. Enterprise MFA transitioning from OTP to FIDO2 (WebAuthn).
questions.realWorld: Google eliminated phishing internally via FIDO2 keys (Krebs on Security 2018 article). Cloudflare survived 2022 Oktapus phishing that took down others thanks to FIDO2. GitHub requires passkey for internal auth. Apple Passkeys iOS 16+ / macOS Ventura. Microsoft Authenticator passkeys. Consumer adoption growing. FIDO Alliance certification for authenticators.

questions.scenario: Dev configura API CORS con `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` porque 'permitía requests desde frontend'.
questions.question: ¿Es problema? ¿Cuándo usar wildcard vs specific origin?

options.text: '*' peligroso if API has credentials (cookies, auth headers, tokens en request headers) — browsers block credentials with wildcard origin. But developers often add Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true — insecure combination. Any origin can invoke API with user's credentials. Better: (1) Specific allowed origins list. (2) Reject unknown origins. (3) If '*' truly needed (public API, no auth), don't allow credentials. CORS es security boundary del browser — enforce it correctly.
options.why: Correcto. CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is browser mechanism relaxing Same-Origin Policy. Access-Control-Allow-Origin controls who can access. '*' means any origin. Combined con Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true = ANY origin can make credentialed request with user's cookies/tokens. Este combination is INSECURE and modern browsers actually block it (must have specific origin for credentials). Correct: whitelist specific origins (frontend domain). Reject unknown. Not add credentials without specific origin.

options.text: '*' siempre safe.
options.why: Falso combined con credentials. Y for private APIs, allowing '*' means any site can invoke your API from user's browser (with their session if any). Restrict appropriately.

options.text: CORS es solo frontend concern.
options.why: Configured en backend response headers. Frontend triggers preflight, backend must respond correctly. Backend responsibility.

options.text: CORS previene CSRF.
options.why: Diferente threat. CORS controls JS invoking cross-origin APIs. CSRF is form submission tricks. CSRF tokens (per-form) or SameSite cookies prevent CSRF. Different mechanism.

questions.explanation: CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing): browser mechanism controlling cross-origin AJAX/fetch requests. By default, SOP (Same-Origin Policy) blocks JS from one origin reading responses from another origin. CORS relaxes conditionally. Server sends response headers: (a) Access-Control-Allow-Origin: origin or * — whose requests allowed. (b) Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true/false — send cookies/auth. (c) Access-Control-Allow-Methods, -Headers, -Max-Age — for preflight. Preflight: OPTIONS request for 'non-simple' requests (custom headers, non-GET/POST/HEAD, JSON content-type). Server must respond with allow headers. Common mistakes: (1) '*' + credentials — browsers reject. (2) Missing headers on OPTIONS — preflight fails, request never sent. (3) Overly permissive — allows any origin to invoke your API. (4) Reflecting Origin header without validation — attacker sets any origin. Best practices: (1) Whitelist specific allowed origins (config). Reject unknown. (2) Don't allow credentials with wildcard. (3) Handle preflight correctly. (4) Consider allowed headers/methods carefully. (5) Age max-age for preflight cache (avoid repeat requests). Similar: CORP (Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy), COEP, COOP for opt-in isolation. CORS enforced only by browsers — doesn't protect against direct API calls (curl, other clients). For that: auth, rate limiting, WAF.
questions.realWorld: Common misconfig in APIs, especially early startups. Security scanners (OWASP ZAP) flag. Bug bounties frequently report CORS misconfig. CSRF token + SameSite cookie combined for CSRF. CORS specifically for XHR/fetch cross-origin. Read MDN CORS documentation.

questions.scenario: Team deployea containers en Kubernetes. Security auditor pregunta sobre container hardening.
questions.question: ¿Cuáles son best practices para container security?

options.text: Distroless o minimal base images (Chainguard, Google distroless, Alpine): reduce attack surface (no shell, no unnecessary tools). Smaller CVE exposure.
options.why: Correcto. Full OS containers (Ubuntu, CentOS) have hundreds of packages, many with CVEs, most unused. Distroless (no shell, minimal packages, just runtime dependencies) drastically reduces attack surface. Chainguard Images maintained low-CVE. Google distroless popular. Alpine small but musl libc caveat. Balance: small = fewer bugs, but breakage risk with unusual dependencies.

options.text: Run as non-root user (USER instruction en Dockerfile, runAsNonRoot: true en Pod).
options.why: Correcto. Container escape vulnerabilities more dangerous con root. runAsUser: 1000, runAsGroup: 1000 (or specific), runAsNonRoot: true. Kubernetes PodSecurityStandards 'Restricted' enforces. Also read-only rootfs (readOnlyRootFilesystem: true) prevents malware install.

options.text: Image scanning en CI (Trivy, Snyk, Grype) — fail build en critical CVEs.
options.why: Correcto. Scan container images para CVEs. Detect vulnerable dependencies. Trivy (Aqua, open-source), Snyk (SaaS), Grype (Anchore), Docker Scout. Integrate into CI — fail builds con critical CVEs. Runtime scanning también (admission control, deployed image scanning).

options.text: Signed images (Sigstore/Cosign): admission controller verifies signature before allowing deploy.
options.why: Correcto. Sigstore/Cosign for image signing. Attestation of who built + what commit. Admission controller (Kyverno, Connaisseur) verifies signature at deploy — prevents unsigned/tampered images running. Supply chain security foundational.

options.text: Latest tag para siempre have newest.
options.why: Anti-pattern. Non-deterministic — new pods may pull different content bajo 'latest'. Breaks GitOps. Use immutable tags (SHA, semver). Renovate/Dependabot updates tags.

questions.explanation: Container security best practices: (1) Base image hardening — distroless, alpine, or Chainguard. Fewer packages = fewer CVEs = smaller attack surface. (2) User — run as non-root (USER 1000). Non-root con capabilities dropped where possible. (3) Read-only rootfs — readOnlyRootFilesystem: true. Writable volumes for state as needed. Prevents malware install. (4) No privileged — privileged: true = kernel access. Only if truly required. (5) Capabilities — drop ALL, add specific (NET_ADMIN if needed). (6) SecurityContext — comprehensive (runAsNonRoot, allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, capabilities.drop). (7) Image scanning — SCA (dependencies) + IaC scanning. CI + runtime. Trivy, Snyk, Grype, Docker Scout. (8) Image signing — Sigstore/Cosign, sign at build, verify at deploy. Kyverno/Connaisseur enforce. (9) Registry security — private registry (ECR, GCR, Harbor). Scan on push. Pull secrets managed. (10) Runtime security — Falco/Tetragon detect anomalies (unexpected syscalls, network). (11) Network policies — segment container network. Default deny + explicit allow. (12) Resource limits — prevent DoS (fork bomb, memory hog). (13) Immutable containers — no exec into prod containers. Use ephemeral debug containers. Comprehensive.
questions.realWorld: Chainguard Images (2022+) launched enterprise-grade low-CVE images. Google distroless widespread. NSA/CISA Kubernetes Hardening Guide covers. Kubernetes PodSecurityStandards (successor to PSP) enforce baseline. Sigstore adoption growing. Google/Cloudflare/major players use signed images with enforcement.

questions.scenario: Post-incident, forensics team pregunta: '¿qué APIs consultaron los credenciales comprometidos entre día X y Y?'. Team not sure — logs incomplete, retention 7 días.
questions.question: ¿Cuáles son requisitos de audit logging para forensics?

options.text: Comprehensive audit logging: (1) All authz decisions (who tried what, allowed/denied). (2) All admin actions (config changes, user creation). (3) Data access to sensitive resources. (4) Immutable storage — logs cannot be tampered by attacker who compromised auth. WORM (S3 Object Lock, Splunk index-lock) or separate account. (5) Retention long enough for compliance + typical dwell time — 90 días minimum, 1-7 años often required (SOC2, HIPAA, GDPR). (6) Integrity — logs signed/hashed. (7) Aggregation — SIEM (Splunk, Elastic, Datadog) para querying. (8) Alerting — anomaly detection.
options.why: Correcto. Audit logs are critical para forensics + compliance. Requirements: (1) Comprehensive — auth events, data access, admin actions. Not just errors — also successful ops. (2) Immutable — attacker gaining admin should not delete logs of their activity. WORM storage, separate log account. (3) Retention — 90d minimum, often 1-7 years by regulation. Compressed archive for cold storage. (4) Integrity — cryptographic hash chains (SigStore for logs, tamper-evident). (5) Aggregation — SIEM centralizes. Enables querying across services. (6) Alerting on anomalies — sudden data access spike, admin login from unusual location. (7) PII redaction — logs shouldn't contain plaintext passwords, keys. Careful of what's logged.

options.text: Log solo errors — success ops no need audit.
options.why: Success ops need audit tan much or MORE. Attacker successful actions blend in. Need to track legitimate ops to detect anomalies + reconstruct timeline. Compliance requires success logging (SOX, PCI).

options.text: Retention 7 days sufficient.
options.why: Insufficient. Average dwell time (breach to detection) is months (~200 days Mandiant reports). Investigation requires historical data. Compliance (HIPAA 6 years, SOC2 typically 1+ year, PCI 1 year online + 3 archive) exceeds 7 days significantly.

options.text: Logs en misma DB que app.
options.why: If attacker compromises app, can modify logs. Logs should be separate storage (S3 Object Lock, CloudTrail immutable, separate account) to prevent tampering.

questions.explanation: Audit logging + forensics architecture: (1) Log sources — application logs (auth events, business transactions), system logs (OS, network), cloud provider (CloudTrail for AWS, Cloud Audit Logs for GCP, Azure Activity Logs), Kubernetes audit logs, container runtime logs. (2) Contents — timestamp, principal (user/service), action, resource, result (allow/deny), source IP, request ID. (3) Storage — immutable (S3 Object Lock, WORM), long retention, encrypted. Consider separate account/tenant for isolation from attacker. (4) Integrity — cryptographic hash chains, signed batches, or SIEM integrity. (5) Aggregation — SIEM (Splunk, Elastic Security, Datadog SIEM, Sentinel, Sumo Logic). Central query. (6) Retention — 90 days minimum for investigation. Compliance may require years. Cold storage for archival. (7) Alerting — anomaly detection, correlation rules. UEBA (User and Entity Behavior Analytics). (8) Access control — audit logs sensitive, restrict access, log access to audit logs (meta). (9) Regulatory — GDPR right to erasure vs retention conflict — usually retention wins for security logs (legitimate interest). Compliance: PCI DSS Req 10 (audit trail), HIPAA §164.312(b) (audit controls), SOX Section 404, SOC2 CC7.2 (system monitoring), GDPR breach notification (72h — requires knowing what happened). Modern: Threat hunting proactive using logs.
questions.realWorld: Solarwinds (2020): attackers persisted 9+ months. Adequate audit logs crucial to reconstruct scope. Target (2013): logs contained alerts, ignored. Uber (2016): logs not preserved adequately. Post-breach forensics dictate legal outcomes (notifications required, regulatory fines). SIEM market $5B+ industry. MITRE ATT&CK framework maps attacker techniques to log signatures.

references.title: NIST SP 800-92 — 'Guide to Computer Security Log Management'

questions.scenario: Team debate: framework nuevo should have security features 'opt-in' or 'opt-out'?
questions.question: ¿Cuál es principio moderno y por qué?

options.text: Secure by default (opt-out): features de security enabled por default, deshabilitables si truly needed. Reasoning: (1) Most users no expert security — mistakes made when opt-in. (2) Default configurations tend to persist en production. (3) Reduces cognitive load — 'safe unless intentional'. Examples: Rails CSRF token default, Django SECURE_* defaults, Kubernetes NetworkPolicy default-deny (some distros), HTTPS-only cookies default. Opt-out documented and deliberate.
options.why: Correcto. Secure by default is universally accepted best practice. Reasoning: (1) Human factor — most developers not security experts. Opt-in misses configurations. (2) Persistence — 'temporary' insecure defaults become permanent. (3) Cognitive load — 'safe unless intentional' vs 'unsafe unless remembered'. (4) Fail-safe defaults (Saltzer-Schroeder 1975 fundamental security principle #1). Examples: Rails CSRF tokens default, Django SECURE_* defaults, K8s RBAC deny by default, cookies HttpOnly/Secure/SameSite defaults, TLS 1.3 default. Modern frameworks Rails, Django, Rust are secure by default. Old JS frameworks less so. Design principle.

options.text: Opt-in — user should choose intentionally.
options.why: Opt-in security fails because users forget, don't know, or defer. 'Insecure by default' historically caused massive breaches. Industry consensus: secure by default.

options.text: Depends on framework.
options.why: Universal principle — all frameworks should be secure by default. Not context-dependent.

options.text: Opt-in mejor for advanced users.
options.why: Advanced users can opt-out from secure defaults. Users who need advanced config understand implications. Secure default doesn't limit advanced — enables safety for non-experts.

questions.explanation: Secure by default is one of Saltzer-Schroeder's 1975 fundamental security principles: 'fail-safe defaults'. Principles include: (1) Least privilege. (2) Fail-safe defaults (secure by default). (3) Economy of mechanism. (4) Complete mediation. (5) Open design. (6) Separation of privilege. (7) Least common mechanism. (8) Psychological acceptability. Modern manifestations: (a) Zero trust — no implicit trust. (b) Defense in depth — layered. (c) Secure by default configs. Framework examples: (1) Rails: CSRF token in forms default, XSS protection in ERB default, SQL escape via ActiveRecord default. (2) Django: SECURE_HSTS_SECONDS, SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT, CSRF middleware default. (3) Modern JS frameworks: React JSX escapes by default. (4) Cookies: recent HTTP standards default SameSite=Lax. (5) Cloud services: S3 blocks public access by default (2018+ change post many breaches), private RDS by default. (6) HTTPS enforcement (RFC 8446 TLS 1.3 defaults). Opposite: Windows XP admin default, MongoDB open port default (2015 breaches). Industry learned. Modern software design: fail closed, secure default, opt-out to relax with explicit documentation. Principle of least astonishment — expected behavior should be safe.
questions.realWorld: AWS S3 changed default to block public access after many breaches (2018+). MongoDB changed default authentication (post-2015 breaches exposed thousands of DBs). React JSX escaping. Cloud SQL default private. Every generation of software moves toward secure defaults after breaches teach.

references.title: Saltzer, Schroeder — 'The Protection of Information in Computer Systems', 1975

questions.scenario: Team achieves SOC2 certification. Manager says: 'now we're secure, don't need to spend more on security'.
questions.question: ¿Es correcto? ¿Qué principio explica la realidad?

options.text: Sí, certification means secure.
options.why: Certification is snapshot of controls at moment. Threats evolve, new vulnerabilities emerge, employees change, config drifts. Security is ongoing.

options.text: Security is a PROCESS, not a state. Threats evolve constantly (new CVEs weekly, new attack techniques, new attacker groups). Security requires: (1) Continuous monitoring, (2) Regular audits, (3) Patch management, (4) Threat intelligence, (5) Training, (6) Incident response readiness, (7) Recurring compliance recertification. SOC2 audit is annual — controls audited, gaps found, remediated iteratively. 'Secure' is never a final state.
options.why: Correcto. Bruce Schneier famously: 'Security is a process, not a product'. Reasons: (1) Threats evolve — new CVEs published daily (NVD). New attack techniques emerge (Log4Shell 2021, novel supply chain 2020). (2) Software changes — every release introduces new risks. (3) People change — employees leave, credentials should be rotated. (4) Config drift — infrastructure changes over time. (5) Compliance is continuous — audits recur, controls must be maintained. SOC2 audit is annual snapshot. Security programs run 365 days. Kaizen (continuous improvement) applies to security.

options.text: Once secure, no need to invest more.
options.why: Not sustainable. Threats evolve. Insecurity accumulates without maintenance. Business changes create new attack surface.

options.text: Certification transfers security responsibility to auditor.
options.why: Auditor validates controls at moment. Ongoing security is your responsibility. Cloud shared responsibility model similar — provider secures infra, you secure your workload.

questions.explanation: Security as a process principle (Bruce Schneier 1998): 'Security is a process, not a product'. Reasons: (1) Adversarial dynamics — attackers evolve techniques as defenses improve. Arms race. (2) New vulnerabilities — CVE published daily. Software you use today has undiscovered bugs. (3) Threat landscape — new attacker groups (nation-state, ransomware gangs), new motivations. (4) Business changes — new features = new attack surface. (5) People — hiring, offboarding, insider threat, training. (6) Technology changes — cloud migrations, new architectures. (7) Compliance is recurring — SOC2 annual, PCI quarterly scans, GDPR ongoing. Continuous activities: (a) Patch management — apply patches for CVEs. (b) Vulnerability scanning — DAST, SAST, dependency scanning. (c) Threat intelligence — monitor for threats targeting your industry. (d) Incident response drills — tabletop exercises. (e) Training — security awareness, phishing simulations. (f) Access review — quarterly access reviews. (g) Monitoring — SIEM alerts, anomaly detection. (h) Chaos engineering — for resilience. (i) Third-party risk — vendor assessments. Frameworks: NIST Cybersecurity Framework (Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover) captures this cycle. ISO 27001 requires continuous improvement (PDCA — Plan, Do, Check, Act). Certification is validation, not endpoint.
questions.realWorld: SolarWinds, Target, Equifax all had compliance certifications when breached. Certification is minimum, not sufficient. Security programs at Facebook, Microsoft, Google run continuously with 100s of engineers. Startups often mistake certification for security state. Post-breach investigation typically finds known issues not remediated.

references.title: Bruce Schneier — 'Security is a Process, Not a Product' (1998)
